9001.gloss: Workday published a Secretariat analysis of HiredScore Spotlight but expressly says it does not satisfy any customer's legal obligation and takes no position on whether Spotlight is an AEDT
9001.verbatim: Workday's own legal page "Responsible AI and Bias Mitigation for HiredScore Spotlight" (workday.com, undated page carrying 2026 test data) says Workday asked Secretariat, an independent third party, to analyse Workday's own deployment of HiredScore Spotlight using Workday's applicant flow data, and that it is publishing a summary of that analysis. The page carries two explicit disclaimers in Workday's words: "This page is provided for transparency purposes only. It is not intended to satisfy any customer-specific legal or regulatory obligation, nor does it suggest or imply that HiredScore Spotlight is or is not an automated employment decision tool under any particular law." It also states the results are specific to Workday's own implementation and that "Outcomes may differ in other settings depending on job requirements, candidate pools, workflow design, configuration choices, and human review processes." So the page functions as vendor transparency, not as a customer-usable Local Law 144 audit summary, and Workday does not concede AEDT status for the tool.

9002.gloss: The exact scope and dates of Workday's Secretariat analysis: testing completed 20 March 2026, distribution date Sept 2025 to Feb 2026, five job profiles, Workday's own NYC-area applicants
9002.verbatim: Workday's responsible-AI page (workday.com) gives the analytic results summary for its HiredScore Spotlight analysis by Secretariat: Date of Testing Completion 20 March 2026; Distribution Date 1 September 2025 to 28 February 2026. The data described is "Spotlight simplified output showing match grades for candidates reported qualifications against Workday's specific job requirements, in an A, B, C, D grading system where A indicates the closest match." The analysis used a sample of Workday's own applicant data from the most recent six months of Spotlight deployment at the time of analysis; the analytic dataset covers applications from U.S. residents for positions in the greater New York City area submitted between 1 September 2025 and 28 February 2026, and only the five job profiles with the highest volume were included. The page says the analysis assessed outcomes across demographic groups using comparative ratios "used to identify whether differences may warrant further review", and includes candidate volume and outcome-rate information by demographic category. It is Workday's own hiring data, not customer deployments.

9003.gloss: A federal judge ordered Workday to identify every customer that enabled HiredScore AI features, after Workday said identifying them posed logistical hurdles
9003.verbatim: HR Dive reported on 31 July 2025 (reporter Caroline Colvin) that a judge in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California ruled Workday Inc. must provide a list of customers who enabled HiredScore artificial intelligence features in their hiring process, even though Workday acquired the technology after the original complaint was filed. The collective action alleges the AI-based applicant recommendation software negatively affected candidates aged 40 and up. The order calls for the collective to include "individuals whose applications were scored, sorted, ranked, or screened using the HiredScore AI features", rejecting Workday's position that the collective should cover only people scored or ranked by its Candidate Skills Match. Workday argued there were "material differences in the scoring algorithms between the HiredScore AI features and Candidate Skills Match" and that HiredScore was "a separate product, built on a wholly separate technology platform" that can run on any applicant tracking software. Per May court documents, "Workday has raised concerns that there may be logistical hurdles to identifying members of the collective", to which Judge Rita Lin said "On the current record, those challenges do not appear insurmountable." Workday had to propose a timeline for identifying those customers by 20 August 2025.

9004.gloss: The compliance file a vendor must hand a customer: a controlled summary template, a field map, and a record of tool version and distribution date, with the customer still owning the public posting
9004.verbatim: A LinkedIn article by Santosh Singh, "New York City Local Law 144: The AI Hiring Compliance File" (published 21 July 2026), sets out what an AI hiring vendor has to supply so a customer can actually deploy in NYC. It says many product teams "stop too early" by preparing an internal test report but not a customer-ready publication package, and that the vendor should give the customer "a controlled summary template, a field map for the underlying data, and a record of the tool version and distribution date covered by the audit", while "The customer still owns the public posting obligation. The vendor must make the information usable." On the notice workflow, it says the contract and implementation materials should state who identifies the New York City use case, who supplies the candidate location, and who activates the notice process, because "A vendor should not leave the customer to guess whether a remote candidate, a New York office, or an employment-agency arrangement triggers the workflow." It also notes imputed or inferred demographic information cannot be used for the audit, creating a product requirement that the vendor support an auditor "without silently inventing missing demographic data or hiding unknown categories inside an overall result." The article's framing line: "An AI product that cannot produce that evidence is difficult for a customer to deploy in New York City, even if the model performs well in a technical evaluation."

9005.gloss: What the LL144 candidate notice must contain and when it must be delivered: five specified elements, at least 10 business days before use, by posting, mail or email
9005.verbatim: The same LinkedIn compliance article by Santosh Singh (21 July 2026) states that candidates and employees who reside in New York City must receive notice that an AEDT will be used and notice of the job qualifications or characteristics the tool will assess, and that the notice must include instructions for requesting a reasonable accommodation under other applicable laws. Citing the DCWP FAQ, it says the notice must be provided at least 10 business days before the AEDT is used, and may be delivered in a job posting, by mail, or by email, with specified website or written-policy approaches allowed in some situations. It also confirms the law took effect on 1 January 2023 and DCWP began enforcement on 5 July 2023, and describes the law as connecting the model to a chain of evidence: the employment decision the tool supports, the data and categories used to test it, the audit and public summary, the notice given to the candidate or employee, and "the records that show which version of the tool was used."

9006.gloss: The law puts no direct obligation on vendors, so a customer's ability to comply depends on the contract, and a current vendor audit can sometimes be reused
9006.verbatim: VerifyWise's "NYC Local Law 144: bias audit and AEDT checklist" (published 13 February 2026, updated 12 June 2026) tells employers to inventory every tool touching candidate evaluation, documenting the tool name and vendor, what it does, what data it ingests, whether it produces a score/classification/recommendation, and whether that output substantially assists or replaces a human decision. It states plainly: "If a vendor provides the tool, contact them about their Local Law 144 compliance posture. Note that the law does not impose direct obligations on vendors, so cooperation depends on your contractual relationship." On reuse, it says a vendor can have an independent auditor conduct a bias audit on its tool and share those results, and "If your vendor already has a current audit, you may be able to use it rather than commissioning your own, provided it covers the same tool configuration you deploy" — and that a vendor cannot audit its own tool, though it can coordinate data collection for a third-party auditor. It also notes many companies are surprised to find AEDTs embedded in applicant tracking systems, recruitment marketing platforms, or assessment providers they assumed were purely manual.

9007.gloss: The four things a customer must operate: annual audit, published summary, a 10-business-day notice per candidate, and annual renewal
9007.verbatim: VerifyWise's Local Law 144 checklist (published 13 February 2026, updated 12 June 2026) breaks compliance into four operating steps: (1) an annual independent bias audit covering selection rates, impact ratios and intersectional cross-tabs across the required demographic categories; (2) a public results summary on the employer's own website covering the audit date, distribution date and source data description; (3) a 10-day candidate notice — "Each candidate must be notified at least 10 business days before the AEDT is used to evaluate them"; and (4) annual renewal, because audits expire after 12 months and new audits are needed before expiration and when models or data materially change. The published summary must include the date of the most recent bias audit, the distribution of results across required demographic categories, the source and explanation of the data used, and the number of individuals assessed by the AEDT. The notice itself must state that an AEDT will be used, the job qualifications and characteristics it will evaluate, the type of data collected, the source of the data, and the data retention policy, and candidates must be informed of their right to request an alternative selection process or accommodation where reasonably available. Notice can be given in the job posting itself or in a separate written communication at least 10 business days before.

9008.gloss: Employers cannot comply without vendor cooperation: they need the vendor's audit-ready data and model documentation, and audit documentation is now a procurement gate
9008.verbatim: Warden AI's vendor playbook "NYC LL 144 for HR Tech Vendors" by Jeffrey Pole (published 4 June 2026, updated 9 July 2026) states that LL 144 "does not regulate vendors by name. It regulates the employers and employment agencies that deploy your product", but that "no employer can comply without vendor cooperation — the audit obligation sits on the contract surface between you and your customer." Specifically: "The employer needs your audit-ready data, your model documentation, and in most cases a vendor-coordinated audit their internal teams can rely on." It argues the "we just build the tool" posture is collapsing commercially: "A vendor that cannot produce a current third-party bias audit forces the buyer to commission one independently — at the buyer's cost, on the buyer's timeline, and with the buyer's chosen audit firm", and audit documentation "has moved from differentiator to gate" in enterprise procurement. On the litigation side it says Mobley v. Workday's procedural ruling — that Workday, the vendor rather than the employer, can be held liable as an "agent" of the employers using its tool — cleared the path for collective treatment, so "The exposure is not capped at one customer's hiring volume. It is the aggregate of every applicant ever screened by the in-scope tool, across every customer." It also notes DCWP enforcement has been comparatively quiet since July 2023, with penalties of $500 for a first violation and $1,500 per day for each day a non-compliant AEDT remains in use.

9009.gloss: A contrasting vendor posture: Bryq contracted Holistic AI and makes a Summary Results report dated 15 May 2023 available to customers on request
9009.verbatim: Assessment vendor Bryq's help-centre article "Bryq Compliance according to NYC Local Law 144" (dated 9 February 2026) states directly that the law "applies to you if you use Bryq's AI-powered automated candidate ranking functionality within your hiring process", and answers the vendor-audit question affirmatively: "we have contracted Holistic AI, a leading AI audit and risk management firm. A Summary Results report produced on May, 15th of 2023 is available to customers upon request." It also points customers to a separate published guidance document, "Guidelines for Customers on New York City Local Law 144 of 2021", covering their obligations for the use of automated employment decision tools. The article notes the law was enacted in 2021 with enforcement pushed from 1 January 2023 to 15 April 2023 and finally to 5 July 2023, and that it provides no exemptions based on the size or revenue of the employer.

9010.gloss: DCWP itself revised its slides in June 2023 to clarify the notice must come 10 business days before the tool is used
9010.verbatim: The New York City Department of Consumer and Worker Protection's official AEDT page (nyc.gov/site/dca) states that Local Law 144 of 2021 prohibits employers and employment agencies from using an automated employment decision tool unless the tool has been subject to a bias audit within one year of the use of the tool, information about the bias audit is publicly available, and certain notices have been provided to employees or job candidates. It confirms "DCWP will begin enforcement of this law and rule on July 5, 2023." The page also records a specific clarification on the notice timing: after educational roundtables held in May 2023, "DCWP revised the presentation slides in June 2023 to clarify that the Notice must be provided 10 business days prior to use of an AEDT." DCWP takes complaints from candidates who report that an employer or employment agency used an AEDT but did not have the required bias audit done, did not post a summary of the audit results, or did not give the required notices, and no account is needed to file.

9011.gloss: A large employer told DCWP the 10-business-day notice was unworkable at its volume: 368,536 applications for 12,796 posted positions in one year
9011.verbatim: In the public comment record on DCWP's proposed AEDT rules (rules.cityofnewyork.us, comments closed October 2022, 20 online comments), Hannah Wade of NYU Langone Health objected specifically to the notice workflow: "we have concerns about the potential hiring delays presented by the requirement (Section 5-303) to provide notice to candidates and employees 10 business days prior to the use of an automated employment decision tool, or AEDT. This requirement presents an unnecessary waiting period that will prolong staffing shortages." The comment quantifies the scale involved: "During our Fiscal Year 2022, we received 368,536 applications for 12,796 posted positions which require the use of data analytics to effectively process. Delays of 10 business days in processing time would pose an undue hardship on our healthcare system." The same comment record contains an objection from Fred Oswald of Rice University noting that the 4/5ths rule (an impact ratio below .80 as a prima facie case for disparate impact) comes from the UGESP FAQ, is asymmetric, and "is easier to violate at lower selection rates (e.g., 1.5% vs. 2% selection violates the 4/5ths Rule...) than at higher ones (e.g., 76% vs. 95% does not violate the 4/5ths rule, yet is a 19% selection rate difference)."

9012.gloss: The alternative selection process is a fourth standalone requirement, not part of the notice: candidates must get one on request
9012.verbatim: The guide "How to Comply with the NYC Bias Audit Law in 2026" (nycbiasaudit.com, published 30 January 2026) lists four fundamental requirements employers must meet before using an AEDT, treating the alternative path as its own obligation: (1) an independent bias audit conducted within one year before use and renewed annually, by an auditor not involved in developing or using the AEDT; (2) public disclosure of audit results including summary statistics, the date of the audit, and selection rates and impact ratios for protected categories; (3) candidate and employee notification covering the use of an AEDT, the job qualifications and characteristics the tool will assess, and information about data collection, retention and usage policies; and (4) "Alternative Selection Process or Accommodation — Candidates and employees must be provided with an alternative selection process or reasonable accommodation upon request." The guide's compliance sequence starts with Step 1, inventory your AI tools, listing resume screening software, applicant tracking systems with AI components, video interview analysis tools, skills assessment platforms and chatbots used for candidate evaluation as the categories to enumerate. Penalties listed are up to $500 for a first violation and up to $1,500 per subsequent violation, with additional penalties for failure to provide notice.

9013.gloss: No Testlify entry appears in the ACLU/NYCLU crowd-sourced tracker of published Local Law 144 bias audits; the 16 June 2023 BABL AI 'Matching Model' audit belongs to Eightfold.AI
9013.verbatim: The ACLU and NYCLU maintain a public crowd-sourced repository (github.com/aclu-national/tracking-ll144-bias-audits) collecting bias audits employers have posted under NYC Local Law 144, with columns for deploying entity, tool vendor or name, auditor, date of audit, the original link and a Perma.cc capture. The visible tracker lists roughly 30 audit entries covering ADP (ADP Profile Relevance and Candidate Relevancy, BLDS LLC, 04/2023 and 04/2024), Bloomberg (PLUM Assessment, Resolution Economics LLC, 7/3/2023), BNP Paribas (pymetrics/Harver Soft Skills Platform, BABL AI, 6/29/2023), Dover (Varun Ganesan, 6/23/23), Eightfold.AI (Eightfold Matching Model, BABL AI, 6/16/2023 and 4/03/2023), HackerRank (Plagiarism Detection System and Image Analysis System, BABL AI, 6/30/2023 and 7/22/2024), The Hartford (DCI Consulting Group, 7/5/2023), HiredScore (7/2/2023 and 2/12/2024), JetBlue (HireVue assessments, DCI Consulting Group, 7/5/2023 and 7/5/2024), Morgan Stanley (Eightfold Matching Model, BLDS LLC, 7/5/2023 and 7/31/2024), NBCUniversal (SmartRecruiters SmartAssistant, Conductor AI, 7/11/2023), NYU Langone Health (Talent Plus, Ambrose Consulting LLC, 2023), Paradox (Olivia Chatbot and Traitify Tool, Holistic AI, 2023 and 2024), Pfizer (HireVue, DCI Consulting Group, 7/5/2023), Plum (Holistic AI, 8/23/2023), Reejig (Holistic AI, 11/30/2023), RippleMatch (Fit Score Algorithm, BABL AI, 6/22/2023 and 6/27/2024), Sheppard Mullin (Suited Law Assessment, Holistic AI, 5/26/2023 and 3/11/2024), Wells Fargo (DCI Consulting Group, 7/5/2023) and Covey (Conductor AI, 8/10/2023). Testlify does not appear anywhere in that listing. The one audit dated 16 June 2023 of a 'Matching Model' is Eightfold.AI's Eightfold Matching Model, audited by BABL AI, and the ACLU notes it was removed from the employer website as of a check on 9/30/24. The repository's stated reason for existing is that although employers are required to link to the relevant bias audit on their website, 'these audits can be very difficult to find, and some employers have posted and later removed this information' — the tracker flags several such removals, including ADP (removed, captured 11/06/23), HackerRank's 2023 audits (removed as of 9/30/24), The Hartford (removed as of 11/02/23), HiredScore (removed as of 10/1/24), JetBlue's 2023 audit (removed as of 10/1/24), Morgan Stanley's 2023 audit (removed as of 10/1/24), RippleMatch's 2023 audit (removed as of 10/1/24) and Covey (removed as of 9/30/24).

9014.gloss: Citizens Bank's published bias audit summary: 57 of 640 comparisons (8.9%) had impact ratios below 0.80, none of them on gender
9014.verbatim: Citizens (Citizens Bank, N.A.) publishes a 'DCI Audit Summary' on its careers site to satisfy NYC Local Law 144. The AEDT it uses runs 16 different competency-based scoring algorithms, each of which can generate up to 40 comparisons across gender, ethnicity and the intersection of gender and race, allowing for up to 640 total comparisons. In the audit reported on that page, 57 comparisons out of 640 (8.9%) produced an impact ratio below 0.80. Those results were concentrated in the top tier of scores (40 of the sub-0.80 ratios) and in the intersection of gender and ethnicity (42 sub-0.80 ratios, 30 of them from top-tier comparisons, which Citizens attributes partly to those groups being smaller than gender or ethnicity alone). Ethnicity alone produced 15 impact ratios below 0.80, 10 of them from top-tier comparisons. There were no impact ratios below 0.80 for gender. Citizens states the audit is conducted by a third-party auditor and that Local Law 144 does not itself define 'bias' or say what counts as a good or bad passing-rate difference, so Citizens uses the EEOC's four-fifths rule, treating impact ratios below 0.80 as practically significant while calling it 'a helpful benchmark' rather than a definitive indication of bias. The page also warns that apparently large differences can come from instability in small samples, defining a small sample as a group that is less than 2% of the overall applicant population or fewer than 30 individuals, and notes that its published table aggregates data from multiple sources. The summary lists the 16 audited competencies by name, including Adaptability, Communication, Dependability, Drive for Results and Initiative, Negotiation and Persuasion, five Personality scales (Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, Emotional Stability, Extraversion, Openness), Relationship Building, Safety and Compliance Orientation, Service Orientation, Team Orientation and Willingness to Learn.

9015.gloss: What a compliant bias audit table has to contain, in the words of an employer who publishes one
9015.verbatim: Citizens' published Local Law 144 summary spells out the structure a bias audit table must have. A bias audit table 'must account for how various groups were scored by the AI tools', and the tables are sorted by gender, by ethnicity, by the intersection of gender and race, the number of applicants, the 'passing rate' of each group and the 'impact ratio' for each demographic group. Citizens defines passing rate as the percentage of applicants who passed the assessment at a given tier, and impact ratio as the highest-passing group's rate divided into every other group's rate, so the ratio expresses the difference in passing rates between demographics (for example between male and female applicants). These figures have to be provided for each classification of scores the AEDT produces: the tool Citizens uses percentile-ranks scores and groups them into thirds, giving 'bottom', 'middle' and 'top' tiers, and the table then compares passing rates between those three tiers. Citizens also states the audit itself 'considers things like historical applicant demographics and how the AEDTs used by Citizens score job-related competencies', and that the audit is performed by a third-party auditor because the law requires it.

9016.gloss: NYC DCWP: bias audit within one year of use, results posted publicly, notice 10 business days before use, enforcement from 5 July 2023
9016.verbatim: The New York City Department of Consumer and Worker Protection (DCWP) states that Local Law 144 of 2021 prohibits employers and employment agencies from using an automated employment decision tool (AEDT) unless three conditions are met: the tool has been subject to a bias audit within one year of the use of the tool, information about the bias audit is publicly available, and certain notices have been provided to employees or job candidates. DCWP began enforcing the law and its rule on July 5, 2023. The agency ran educational roundtables in May 2023 (with employers on 22 May, with civil and worker rights advocates on 24 May, and with audit industry stakeholders on 25 May) and revised its presentation slides in June 2023 to clarify that the required notice must be provided 10 business days prior to use of an AEDT. DCWP also takes complaints from the public against an employer or employment agency that used an AEDT but did not make sure the required bias audit was done, did not post a summary of the results of the bias audit, or did not give the required notices; no account is needed to file one.

9017.gloss: BABL AI's CEO on how a bias audit is actually run: ISAE 3000, selection rate or scoring rate, and the historical-data vs test-data split
9017.verbatim: Shea Brown, CEO of the independent AI assurance firm BABL AI, published a practitioner account of bias audit methodology on 04/03/2026. BABL AI was founded in 2018, specialises in bias audits for AI hiring tools under NYC Local Law 144 and comparable rules in Colorado, California and the EU, and conducts its engagements under ISAE 3000, the international assurance standard used in financial auditing, with auditors certified through its own internal programme. Brown states that every bias audit starts with a performance metric, and that the most common one for hiring tools is the selection rate: the probability that a candidate who applies is advanced, recommended or selected by the system. Other defensible metrics depending on the tool are false positive rate, false negative rate, true positive rate/recall and score distributions across demographic groups. For NYC Local Law 144 specifically, he writes that the published guidelines require impact ratios derived either from selection rate or from 'scoring rate', which is the rate at which a particular group scores above the median score of the overall applicant pool. On data, the best case is real applicant data with self-declared demographic information, obtained either through arrangements with employer clients who share ATS data for audit purposes or through the vendor's own consented intake process. Where a vendor has little or no demographic data, Local Law 144 calls this a 'test data' scenario, and the options are to infer demographic characteristics from available signals or to source synthetic or representative test data, both of which carry tradeoffs and require documented methodology. Brown adds that scoping decisions — which geographies, industries, job levels and functions the audit covers — must be made and justified, because a tool used for hourly warehouse hiring behaves differently from one used for professional services roles, and that regulators and clients respond poorly to 'a gap with no explanation'.

9018.gloss: The exact demographic categories a Local Law 144 audit must test, the impact ratio formula, and the fines for skipping it
9018.verbatim: A January 30, 2026 compliance guide published by nycbiasaudit.com sets out the four core requirements of NYC Local Law 144: an independent third-party bias audit of any AEDT conducted within one year before its use and renewed annually; public disclosure of the audit information, which must include summary statistics from the audit, the date of the audit, and selection rates and impact ratios for protected categories; notification to candidates and employees that an AEDT is in use, what job qualifications and characteristics it assesses, and the data collection, retention and usage policies; and an alternative selection process or reasonable accommodation on request. Per DCWP, an independent auditor is a person or organisation not involved in developing the AEDT, not involved in using it for employment decisions, and with the expertise to conduct bias audits to regulatory standards. The audit must cover six ethnicity categories (Hispanic or Latino, White, African American, Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander, Asian, Native American or Alaska Native), two sex categories (Male, Female), and the intersectional categories combining sex and ethnicity, such as female Hispanic or male Asian. Selection rate is the proportion of candidates from each demographic category selected by the AEDT; impact ratio is the selection rate for a group divided by the selection rate for the most selected group, with a ratio below 0.80 generally indicating potential adverse impact under the EEOC's four-fifths rule. The guide quotes the EEOC's definition of adverse impact as 'a substantially different rate of selection in hiring, promotion, or other employment decision which works to the disadvantage of a race, sex, or ethnic group.' Penalties run to up to $500 for a first violation and up to $1,500 for subsequent violations, with additional penalties for failure to provide notice, and each use of a non-compliant AEDT could count as a separate violation. The guide names skills assessment platforms and video interview analysis tools explicitly among the AEDTs an employer must inventory, alongside resume screening software, ATS systems with AI components, and chatbots used for candidate evaluation.

9019.gloss: Workday's published Secretariat analysis shows what a dated, scoped vendor disclosure looks like: testing completed 20 March 2026, distribution window 1 Sep 2025 to 28 Feb 2026
9019.verbatim: Workday publishes a 'Responsible AI and Bias Mitigation for HiredScore Spotlight' page describing an analysis it commissioned from Secretariat, an independent third party, of Workday's own deployment of HiredScore Spotlight using Workday's own applicant flow data. The disclosure carries an explicit Date of Testing Completion of March 20, 2026 and a Distribution Date of September 1, 2025 – February 28, 2026. The data collected is described as Spotlight's simplified output showing match grades for candidates' reported qualifications against Workday's specific job requirements, in an A, B, C, D grading system where A indicates the closest match. The analytic dataset was drawn from the most recent six months of Spotlight deployment at the time of analysis and includes applications from U.S. residents for positions in the greater New York City area submitted between September 1, 2025 and February 28, 2026, restricted to the five job profiles with the highest volume. Workday states the published table includes candidate volume and outcome-rate information across relevant demographic categories plus comparative ratios used to identify whether differences may warrant further review. It also carries an explicit scope disclaimer: the page 'is provided for transparency purposes only', is not intended to satisfy any customer-specific legal or regulatory obligation, and does not suggest or imply that HiredScore Spotlight is or is not an automated employment decision tool under any particular law; and because the results come from Workday's own deployment context, they should be understood as specific to that implementation, with outcomes potentially differing elsewhere depending on job requirements, candidate pools, workflow design, configuration choices and human review processes.

9020.gloss: Under LL 144 the audit duty follows the job location, not the employer's headquarters, and it sits with the employer rather than the vendor
9020.verbatim: Warden AI's employer guide to NYC Local Law 144, written by Martyn Redstone, published 08 May 2026 and updated 23 Jun 2026, states that the law requires an annual, independent bias audit for each automated hiring tool, clear notification to candidates, and public disclosure of the audit summary on the employer's website. It stresses that jurisdiction is determined by the location of the job, not the location of the employer: any company using automated tools to screen, score or select candidates for a position based in New York City must comply even if headquartered in another state or country, and this extends to remote roles filled by people working from within the city. The rules took effect on July 5, 2023, ending the grace period, and are enforced by the NYC Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, with financial penalties accruing per violation and accumulating daily. On third-party tools, the guide is explicit that where an employer uses a vendor's AI tool the compliance responsibility ultimately rests with the employer, who must ensure a bias audit has been conducted and post the results publicly, which means reviewing the bias audits and other compliance documentation the vendor provides. The guide also warns that the public disclosure rule is what turns a finding of bias into a lasting exposure, putting it on the record where it can fuel discrimination claims, and that lasting compliance requires a complete inventory of tools, an AI governance framework, and continuous monitoring to catch model drift between annual audit cycles.

9021.gloss: The deliverables a complete bias-audit package should contain, and why a vendor's own analysis does not count as the independent audit
9021.verbatim: Holistic AI's NYC Local Law 144 page lists the deliverables it produces for compliance: an annual bias audit report containing selection rates and impact ratios by protected class; a ready-to-publish public summary of the most recent audit findings; a compliant candidate notice template stating that an AEDT is used; an audit-ready evidence package comprising a scope statement, dataset schema, definitions, results and limitations; a mitigation roadmap with documented actions, owners and timelines for any identified issues; and a repeatable annual process. The page carries an explicit caveat that Local Law 144 requires an independent audit, that Holistic AI supports analysis and documentation, and that 'you may still need a third-party auditor to sign off' — its FAQ repeats that many organisations engage a third-party auditor to demonstrate independence. Its FAQs also define an AEDT as any computational process that substantially assists or replaces human discretion in employment decisions, the key question being whether the tool screens, ranks or scores candidates or employees; state that most audits include selection rates by protected group and impact ratios versus a reference group, with the four-fifths rule (0.8) described as 'the commonly used screening heuristic' and explicitly 'not a universal legal standard'; instruct that missing demographics be tracked as 'unknown / not disclosed' explicitly and never dropped silently, with the approach documented in the audit package; warn that small samples make ratios unstable and that the limitation must be documented clearly, with a longer time window or appropriate aggregation considered; and confirm the law requires annual audits, recommending a clear renewal cadence with a defined data cutoff window. The page is dated by a 2026 copyright line and links resources published between July 2023 and April 2024.

9022.gloss: No scraped page names Testlify — but every source agrees the employer, not the vendor, carries LL 144 liability
9022.verbatim: Fruggr's NYC Local Law 144 compliance guide states plainly that the compliance obligation sits with the employer, not the vendor: "our ATS vendor handles that" is not a defense DCWP recognizes. The law has applied since 5 July 2023 to any employer or employment agency with a physical NYC office using an automated tool to screen or rank candidates for an NYC-based role or a remote role associated with an NYC office. Skills-assessment platforms with algorithmic scoring are named explicitly as tools that qualify as an AEDT. Violations of the audit, notice or posting requirements carry fines of $375 to $1,500 per violation, with each day of continued non-compliance typically treated as a separate violation. The audit itself must be run by an auditor who is not an employee of the company or the vendor, was not involved in developing the AEDT, and holds no direct or material indirect financial interest in either party; it must calculate impact ratios across sex, race/ethnicity and intersectional categories (for example Black women vs white men), using historical usage data or, where unavailable, test data, with imputing candidate demographics prohibited. An audit is valid for exactly one year from the date it was conducted, with no grace period.

9023.gloss: DCWP enforcement is weak, and the state Comptroller found 17 of 32 sampled companies potentially non-compliant against DCWP's one
9023.verbatim: Fruggr, citing a December 2025 audit by the New York State Comptroller's office, reports that NYC's Department of Consumer and Worker Protection received only two AEDT-related complaints between July 2023 and June 2025, and had not investigated whether its own complaint-intake process was working. When DCWP reviewed a sample of 32 companies' websites and bias-audit postings it flagged just one non-compliance issue; when the Comptroller's own audit team reviewed the same 32 companies, they found at least 17 instances of potential non-compliance, more than half the sample. The gap was attributed not to a legal loophole but to DCWP staff lacking the technical background to evaluate AEDTs and not consulting the city's own tech agency. Fruggr's reading: low complaint volume reflects weak detection, not widespread compliance, and as enforcement capacity catches up the exposure for companies that assumed nobody was checking becomes retroactive.

9024.gloss: Three 2026 lawsuits put the vendor itself, not just the employer, on the hook — including an FCRA claim over algorithmic scores
9024.verbatim: A LinkedIn post by Dr. Stacey T., dated around April 2026, summarises three cases it says have moved AI hiring liability "from theory to litigation reality". First, Mobley v. Workday: a federal judge held that AI software vendors can be liable as "agents" of the employer, now proceeding as a nationwide collective action in which the court is identifying which specific AI tools (HiredScore is named) were used to filter candidates. Second, Kistler v. Eightfold AI, a 2026 class action arguing that AI "likelihood of success" scores are effectively consumer reports, so under the Fair Credit Reporting Act candidates must be notified when they are scored by an algorithm; the post notes this claim does not require proving the AI was biased, only that the scoring was undisclosed. Third, xAI v. Colorado, filed 10 April 2026, in which xAI argues that a state law forcing an AI to be unbiased is compelled speech under the First Amendment. The post lists three questions it says buyers should put to a vendor: whether the contract indemnifies the customer against bias claims if the vendor is ruled an agent of the employer; whether candidates are told they are being scored and given a path to dispute the score under FCRA; and when the customer's specific instance of the tool was last independently audited for bias and transparency. It is a practitioner LinkedIn post, not a court record or law-firm client alert.

9025.gloss: Colorado is the only US law placing direct duties on the HR tech vendor itself, not just the employer buying it
9025.verbatim: Warden AI's multi-state compliance guide (by Jeffrey Pole, published 18 June 2026, updated 1 July 2026) counts six US regulations now governing AI in employment decisions, each using its own term: AEDT (NYC LL 144), ADMT (California CCPA and Colorado SB 26-189), ADS (California FEHA), Predictive Data Analytics and AI (Illinois HB 3773), and automated employment-related decision technology (Connecticut SB 5). Colorado SB 26-189 is identified as the only US regulation explicitly imposing direct obligations on both developers (HR tech vendors) and deployers (employers) in a dual structure; every other US regulation places primary obligations on employers and pulls vendors in indirectly. SB 26-189 replaced Colorado's earlier SB 24-205 in May 2026 and takes effect 1 January 2027, using a disclosure-and-human-review model rather than a mandated bias audit, enforced exclusively by the Colorado Attorney General as a deceptive trade practice, with no private right of action; enforcement is currently stayed pending the xAI litigation. NYC LL 144 remains the only US law mandating an annual independent bias audit by name, with penalties from $500 for a first violation to $1,500 per day for each day a non-compliant AEDT stays in use. Connecticut SB 5 writes the audit's value into statute: using an AI tool is not a defense to a discrimination claim, but courts and the Connecticut Commission on Human Rights and Opportunities are directed to weigh anti-bias testing as a mitigating factor.

9026.gloss: The December 2025 Comptroller audit pushed DCWP to formalise enforcement, and law firms are telling clients to expect tighter enforcement through 2026
9026.verbatim: Warden AI's compliance guide (published 18 June 2026) reports that the December 2025 New York State Comptroller audit of DCWP enforcement concluded the agency had been enforcing Local Law 144 ineffectively, and that DCWP has since formalized its enforcement procedures and adopted an internal Enforcement Workbook. Employment-law practices including DLA Piper have advised clients to expect tighter enforcement through 2026 and beyond. The guide also notes that a December 2025 federal preemption executive order promises to flatten the state patchwork, but its scope is being tested in court through xAI's constitutional challenge to Colorado's law, which the DOJ has joined, and the outcome will not be clear until 2027 or beyond. Its conclusion for vendors and employers: independent bias audits are preemption-resistant, because they defend against discrimination liability under federal Title VII regardless of which state statutes survive.

9027.gloss: Buying the tool from a vendor does not transfer the risk: "the vendor said it was unbiased" is not a legal defense
9027.verbatim: Pertama Partners' AI hiring compliance guide (Michael Lansdowne Hauge, 12 August 2025) states that purchasing an AI hiring tool from a third-party vendor does not insulate employers from liability: under Title VII, the ADEA and the ADA the employer remains responsible for discriminatory outcomes, and "the vendor said it was unbiased" is not a legal defense. Its compliance framework puts vendor due diligence as step 4 of six (inventory tools, conduct bias audit, candidate notice and transparency, vendor due diligence, human-in-the-loop safeguards, ongoing monitoring). On NYC LL 144, enforced since April 2023 on its account, it says algorithmically scored personality or skills assessments fall squarely inside the AEDT definition, alongside resume ranking, video interview analysis, screening chatbots and ML-analysed game-based evaluations, while applicant tracking systems that only store and organise applications, scheduling tools, job description generators and non-evaluative sourcing tools fall outside it. The audit must be commissioned from an auditor with no affiliation to the employer or the vendor, conducted no more than one year before the tool is deployed, and published on the employer's public website.

9028.gloss: An employer using an unaudited vendor tool is the one that violates LL 144, and fines run $500 to $1,500 per violation
9028.verbatim: Dorf Nelson & Zauderer LLP's blog on NYC Law 144 (Jon A. Dorf, 18 April 2025) sets out how an HR department falls out of compliance, and its fourth scenario is squarely a vendor problem: a company adopts a hiring tool from a third-party vendor, the vendor claims the tool is AI-based but has not conducted the required bias audit, and the company using it is held responsible for violating Law 144 even though it did not build the tool. Employers must ensure the tools they use comply. The firm lists other failure modes as skipping the annual audit, not notifying candidates ten business days in advance, posting a general "we audited it" statement without the specifics of the results or the corrective actions taken, failing to retain audit documentation for a regulator's review, and finding bias in an audit but taking no corrective action, using the example of a tool with a 15% higher rejection rate for minority candidates than white candidates that the company does not fix. Enforcement sits with DCWP, which can investigate, request bias audit reports, and impose fines ranging from $500 to $1,500 per violation with additional penalties for repeat offenses.

9029.gloss: The proposed DCWP rules never required the independent auditor to be a separate legal entity from the vendor
9029.verbatim: The NYC Rules public comment record for DCWP's proposed Automated Employment Decision Tools rules (comments closed October 2022, 20 online comments) contains a comment from Mike Fetzer, added 18 October 2022, arguing that the proposed definition of independent auditor, "a person or group that is not involved in using or developing an AEDT that is responsible for conducting a bias audit of such AEDT", combined with the rule's own worked example in which a vendor uses historical data collected from employers to conduct the bias audit, indicates that a vendor may conduct the bias audit for the employer as long as the person or group doing it is not the same person or group that developed the AEDT. He notes the same reading lets an employer audit its own use, and that the proposed rules do not require the independent auditor to be a separate legal entity from either the vendor or the employer, asking DCWP to clarify if that was not the intent. A separate comment from Fred Oswald of Rice University argues the four-fifths rule (an impact ratio below 0.80 as a prima facie case of disparate impact), which comes from the UGESP FAQ, is asymmetric and easier to violate at low selection rates, giving the example that 1.5% versus 2% selection breaches it while 76% versus 95%, a 19-point gap, does not. NYU Langone Health commented that it received 368,536 applications for 12,796 posted positions in its fiscal year 2022 and that the ten-business-day notice rule would be an undue hardship.

9030.gloss: What a liability cap actually looks like, and the carve-outs that decide whether a compliance breach is covered
9030.verbatim: LegalOn Technologies' contract guide on limitation of liability clauses explains that such a clause sets the maximum one party can recover from the other, giving the worked example of a manufacturer-retailer deal for electronic devices capping the manufacturer's liability at $1 million. It says these clauses are standard in Master Services Agreements, SaaS terms of service, master purchase agreements and manufacturing and supply agreements, and that in a SaaS agreement the clause protects the provider from excessive damages in a data breach or outage. Its negotiation guidance is that the cap should apply mutually, that the cap can be a fixed amount or based on the contract's value, and that certain conduct should be carved out of it, naming willful misconduct, gross negligence and breaches of confidentiality. Its sample customer-position clause for an MSA excludes special, incidental, consequential and indirect damages for both parties "except to the extent liability arises from (A) the indemnification and defense obligations herein and (B) either party's gross negligence, willful misconduct, or violation of law", and treats losses from breaches of the intellectual property, confidential information and personal information articles as outside that exclusion. It also flags as a defect a clause that says only the provider is shielded from consequential damages rather than both parties.

9031.gloss: DCWP's own AEDT page: the only public complaint channel, and what it accepts complaints about
9031.verbatim: The New York City Department of Consumer and Worker Protection's official AEDT page states that Local Law 144 of 2021 prohibits employers and employment agencies from using an automated employment decision tool unless the tool has been subject to a bias audit within one year of use, information about the bias audit is publicly available, and the required notices have been given to employees or job candidates. DCWP began enforcement of the law and rule on 5 July 2023. Members of the public can file a complaint reporting an employer or employment agency that used an AEDT without the required bias audit, without posting a summary of the audit results, or without giving the required notices, selecting "Employment Agency" or "Other" as the business type; no account is needed to file. DCWP held three educational roundtables in May 2023 (with employers and business advocates on 22 May, civil and worker rights advocates on 24 May, and audit industry stakeholders on 25 May), and revised its presentation slides in June 2023 to clarify that the notice must be provided 10 business days prior to use of an AEDT.

9032.gloss: Jones Walker (Sept 2025) lists five contract provisions AI buyers should demand, plus the market data showing why
9032.verbatim: Jones Walker LLP, in a September 15, 2025 AI Law and Policy Navigator post by partners Jason M. Loring and Lara Sevener titled "AI Vendor Liability Squeeze: Courts Expand Accountability While Contracts Shift Risk," tells legal teams to treat AI vendor negotiations as primary risk-management exercises rather than standard procurement. The five key provisions it names: (1) mutual liability caps rather than one-sided vendor protection; (2) explicit compliance warranties for applicable regulations; (3) audit rights allowing examination of algorithmic decision-making; (4) indemnification for discrimination and bias claims caused by the AI tool; and (5) performance guarantees with measurable metrics. The alert grounds this in market data it cites from legal tech platforms: 88% of AI vendors impose liability caps on themselves, often limiting damages to monthly subscription fees, and only 17% provide warranties for regulatory compliance, which the firm calls a significant departure from standard SaaS practice. It also notes broad indemnification clauses routinely require customers to hold vendors harmless for discriminatory outcomes. The post frames the problem as a "liability squeeze": under the Mobley v. Workday precedent (July 2024, Judge Rita Lin; nationwide class certification May 2025 covering rejected applicants over 40), both the employer and the AI vendor can face discrimination claims, while the typical vendor contract contains liability caps limiting damages to annual fees or a modest multiplier, no or limited compliance warranties on fair hiring, broad indemnification requiring the customer to defend the vendor against discrimination claims, and limited audit rights preventing algorithmic examination for bias.

9033.gloss: Jones Walker (Sept 2025): the governance evidence contracts should be built to produce
9033.verbatim: The same Jones Walker LLP alert of September 15, 2025 argues that internal AI governance is becoming the primary legal defense against discrimination claims, and lists what that governance has to produce: bias testing protocols with documented methodologies and results; regular algorithmic audits by qualified third parties; decision-making transparency with clear human oversight ("human-in-the-loop") procedures; vendor due diligence processes evaluating bias mitigation practices; and impact monitoring systems tracking outcomes across protected classes. On insurance, the firm notes discrimination claims from biased algorithms do not fit neatly into cyber, errors and omissions, or general liability coverage, and advises coverage gap analyses, negotiating specific AI coverage endorsements, considering emerging specialized AI insurance products, and documenting governance practices to support coverage claims. Its blunt summary of the buyer's exposure: the customer becomes legally responsible for discriminatory outcomes caused by algorithms it cannot examine, using training data it cannot audit, with decision logic it cannot fully understand.

9034.gloss: Fisher Phillips (Feb 2025): indemnity language for discrimination costs must be drafted with counsel because public policy often blocks the transfer
9034.verbatim: Fisher Phillips LLP, in a February 14, 2025 Insight titled "Job Applicant Seeks to Expand AI Workplace Screener Lawsuit into a National Class Action," gives employers three procurement instructions on AI hiring tools. First, know what to ask vendors: confirm they follow ethical guidelines and have measures to prevent bias before deployment, including understanding the data used to train their models and the algorithms employed. Second, consider indemnification language: contracts between business partners commonly shift the cost of litigation and resulting damages from employer to vendor, but the firm warns that "public policy doesn't often allow you to transfer the cost of discriminatory behavior to someone else unless the language is carefully constructed," so the clause must be developed with counsel. Third, get an AI governance program in place to set guardrails, monitor outcomes of AI hiring tools regularly, and keep a human touch where needed. The Insight covers the February 6, 2025 filing in which Derek Mobley sought to expand his claim into a nationwide collective covering anyone over 40 rejected by Workday's system since September 2020; four additional named plaintiffs, all over 40, said they had together submitted over 3,000 job applications to Workday-using employers and were rejected from every one, sometimes within minutes and sometimes by emails sent in the middle of the night. Judge Rita Lin set an April 8 hearing on certification.

9035.gloss: Fisher Phillips (July 2024): cap the indemnity by dollar amount or months of damages, and define which vendor behavior it covers
9035.verbatim: Fisher Phillips LLP's July 23, 2024 Insight, "AI Workplace Screener Faces Bias Lawsuit: 5 Lessons for Employers and 5 Lessons for AI Developers," published after the July 12, 2024 order allowing Mobley v. Workday to proceed, gives the most specific drafting guidance of its alerts on indemnity. It advises working with counsel on indemnification language shifting the cost of litigation and damages from employer to vendor, warns again that public policy often will not allow the cost of discriminatory behavior to be transferred, and adds two concrete drafting points: place limits on any such indemnity, "like certain dollar amounts or several months of accrued damages," and make sure the agreement contains specific guidance on what type of vendor behavior falls under it. Beyond indemnity, the firm says employers should consider legal options beyond indemnification if targeted in a discrimination action, including breach of contract claims and deceptive business practice lawsuits to draw the vendor into the litigation. Its other procurement steps: vet vendors on the training data and algorithms with regular audits and evaluations; implement ongoing monitoring of AI hiring outcomes including applicant and hire demographics; and insert human decision-making at critical points, noting that automated screening of check-the-box criteria such as licenses, years of experience and degrees is low risk while fully replacing human judgment on subjective decisions is the riskiest use.

9036.gloss: Fisher Phillips (May 2025): after class certification, demand bias-testing documentation plus contractual assurances on nondiscrimination and data transparency
9036.verbatim: Fisher Phillips LLP's May 20, 2025 Insight on Judge Rita Lin's May 16, 2025 order granting preliminary certification of a nationwide ADEA collective in Mobley v. Workday tells employers to "audit your vendors": ask for documentation showing how their systems are tested for bias, and "require contractual assurances around nondiscrimination and data transparency." The firm's five other steps are: retain human oversight so critical decisions are not made solely by automated tools and train HR teams on when to override algorithmic rankings; document hiring criteria and justifications, watching for tools that rely on vague "fit scores" or unexplainable metrics; monitor for disparate impact by regularly analyzing outcomes across age, race, gender and other protected categories and treating significant disparities as red flags; establish an AI governance program; and track legal shifts. The alert notes the court framed the common question as "whether Workday's AI recommendation system has a disparate impact on applicants over forty" and that the claims will "rise and fall together." It also flags that although President Trump signed an executive order in April 2025 directing federal agencies including the EEOC to eliminate disparate-impact enforcement, that order does not affect private litigation like the Workday case, so employers should expect fewer federal filings but more state agency claims, private class actions and opt-in lawsuits targeting AI tools on disparate-impact grounds.

9037.gloss: Holon Law Partners (Dec 2025): seven AI vendor clauses, including AI-specific carve-outs from liability caps for discriminatory outputs and Local Law 144 transparency support
9037.verbatim: Holon Law Partners, LLP published "The Rise of AI Vendor Agreements: 7 Clauses Every Business Needs to Get Right in 2025" on December 9, 2025. It frames AI vendor agreements as sitting inside a legal landscape that includes Colorado's Artificial Intelligence Act (SB 24-205), the EU AI Act, New York City's automated hiring law (Local Law 144), and a growing wave of copyright and discrimination litigation. The clause set: data rights and ownership (define what customer data the vendor can access, how it can be used, and whether derivative data such as embeddings, logs and fine-tuning outputs belong to the customer, with "no training," "no commingling" or "no retention" provisions where appropriate); model training, fine-tuning and improvement restrictions (whether the vendor can train general-purpose or commercial models on your data, whether fine-tuned models are siloed to your environment, whether the vendor retains rights to apply learnings elsewhere); output rights and IP allocation; liability caps and AI-specific risk carve-outs; security controls and model access; and transparency, documentation and explainability. On liability, the firm names discriminatory or biased outputs, particularly in hiring, lending and insurance, as an AI-specific risk category traditional SaaS caps do not cover, and advises adjusting liability caps for AI-specific harms, carving categories such as data breaches, IP infringement, willful misconduct and regulatory fines out of limitations on liability, and aligning indemnity obligations with where the risk is actually created (training corpus vs customer prompts vs deployment choices). It cites Mobley v. Workday as the illustration of AI-driven decisions becoming a liability focal point for both vendor and customer. On transparency, it points to NYC Local Law 144 as mandating bias audits, public summaries of audit results and candidate notice for automated employment decision tools, to Colorado SB 24-205's duty of "reasonable care" on developers and deployers of high-risk AI with documentation, disclosure and impact assessment obligations, and to the EU AI Act's requirements for high-risk systems on data governance, logging, transparency and human oversight, concluding that vendor agreements increasingly need to require access to model documentation including known limitations. It also references the NIST AI Risk Management Framework as calling for documentation, monitoring and controls across the AI lifecycle, and lists security items for the contract: encryption, access control and environment isolation; logging and monitoring of model access and abuse; incident response timelines and cooperation duties; restrictions on subcontractors and infrastructure providers; and controls over how test, support and debugging environments handle real data.

9038.gloss: Stanford CodeX (March 2025): TermScout contract data — 88% of AI vendors cap their own liability, only 17% commit to full regulatory compliance, 92% claim broad data rights
9038.verbatim: Stanford Law School's CodeX blog published "Navigating AI Vendor Contracts and the Future of Law: A Guide for Legal Tech Innovators" by CodeX affiliate Olga Mack on March 21, 2025, drawing on data from TermScout, a contract certification platform that evaluates the fairness of tech contracts, comparing a sampling of AI vendor contracts against traditional SaaS agreements. The findings: 88% of AI vendors impose liability caps on themselves, close to the broader SaaS figure of 81%, but only 38% cap customer liability compared with 44% in broader SaaS, an imbalance that shifts financial and legal burdens onto customers and can leave them with limited recourse for AI failures including biased hiring decisions. Only 17% of AI contracts in the study included warranties related to compliance with documentation, against 42% in SaaS contracts. Only 17% explicitly commit to complying with all applicable laws, against 36% in SaaS agreements, which forces companies to assume responsibility for bias mitigation and regulatory compliance even when using external systems. 92% of AI contracts claim data usage rights beyond what is necessary for service delivery, far above the market average of 63%, with many contracts allowing vendors to use customer data for retraining models or competitive intelligence. Just 33% provide indemnification for third-party IP claims. The piece recommends linking warranties to specific performance metrics and reliability standards, with remedies such as model retraining or service credits for non-compliance, and notes vendors argue AI's probabilistic nature makes rigid warranties hard to enforce, suggesting tiered warranties based on complexity or insurance-backed protections as a middle path.

9039.gloss: Privacy counsel David Arrick (March 2025): mandatory audit rights, disclosure of model changes, and a defined process for biases found during audits
9039.verbatim: David Arrick, a privacy and AI governance lawyer (CIPP/US), published "Top 3 Considerations for Lawyers in AI Vendor Contracts" on LinkedIn on March 28, 2025, naming three high-risk provisions to negotiate. On audit and transparency rights, he notes AI vendors often resist granting customers audit rights over models and data usage, leaving the buyer unable to assess how the AI processes personal data, whether biases exist, or whether security vulnerabilities emerge over time. His four asks: include mandatory audit rights allowing regular compliance reviews; require vendors to provide explanations of AI decision-making to comply with GDPR's right to explanation; demand disclosure of AI model changes that impact data processing and compliance; and establish a clear process for handling AI-generated errors or biases detected during audits. On indemnification and liability, he says many AI contracts disclaim liability for privacy violations, leaving the customer holding regulatory fines and third-party claims from AI-generated decisions, and advises securing indemnification covering regulatory fines and third-party claims, avoiding liability caps that exclude AI-related privacy breaches, requiring vendors to carry cyber insurance covering AI-related compliance risks, and clarifying the vendor's duty to notify customers of potential privacy risks. On data usage rights, he advises explicitly limiting AI training rights to anonymized or synthetic data, requiring express approval before any secondary use, specifying post-contract data deletion obligations, and including geographical restrictions on data storage and processing.

9040.gloss: AI GRC director Hernan Huwyler: a four-layer AI contracting framework with AI-specific service levels and fairness metrics instead of uptime-only SLAs
9040.verbatim: Prof. Hernan Huwyler, MBA CPA CAIO, an AI GRC director and compliance auditor, sets out a four-layer framework for negotiating AI vendor agreements in "How to Negotiate AI Agreements That Protect Data, Value, and Liability" (published March 15, 2026 on his AI Governance and Risk Management blog). The layers: data and output rights; risk and liability allocation; operational performance controls; and lifecycle protections. He argues AI vendor contracts are still written as if AI were ordinary SaaS, that standard terms favor the vendor heavily, and that many cap liability so low the customer carries most of the AI-specific risk. On operational performance he is specific that traditional uptime-only SLAs are not enough: the contract should define AI-specific service levels, drift management, quality thresholds, fairness metrics, update controls and practical remedies for underperformance, and these measurable obligations should be defined before procurement signs, not after implementation problems appear. On liability he says the vendor should not be able to market the system as suitable for a specific workflow, disclaim meaningful output responsibility, and still rely on a tiny liability cap when the system fails in a predictable AI-specific way, naming discriminatory outputs alongside hallucinations, privacy leakage and IP infringement as the failure modes at issue; the critical artifacts to negotiate are the liability clause, indemnity clauses, limitation language, carve-outs, insurance requirements, and the product claims made in sales materials. His test for the whole deal: "Who creates the risk and who pays when it materializes? If the answers do not align, redraft." On data he advises narrowing the vendor's rights to use customer data for model training, product development, profiling or unrelated analytics, and separating raw data, prompts, outputs, logs, embeddings and fine-tuned derivatives in the contract rather than treating them loosely. On lifecycle he warns AI lock-in is more dangerous than ordinary software lock-in because the vendor may hold embeddings, fine-tuned behavior and retrieval structures, and that termination rights are leverage from the first draft.

9041.gloss: Bloomberg Law (July 2024): the agent theory that makes vendor-facing contract terms matter, and the line the court drew between a screening tool and a spreadsheet
9041.verbatim: Bloomberg Law's Daily Labor Report published "Employers Find Openings to Share AI Bias Liability With Vendors" by Lilah Burke on July 15, 2024, reporting that employers hit with hiring bias lawsuits are getting openings to share liability with the vendors that build the tools. Todd Horn, a partner at Venable LLP, is quoted: "Typically, vendors who provide selection tools don't view themselves as really part of the employment process. There has been in recent years a bigger push to hold the vendors of selection tools liable under employment discrimination laws as an agent of the employer." On July 12, 2024, Judge Rita Lin of the US District Court for the Northern District of California allowed some of Mobley's bias claims to proceed on the argument that Workday could be liable as an agent of its employer-customers, finding the complaint adequately alleged those customers delegated traditional employment tasks to Workday. Lin drew the line between Workday and a vendor providing a spreadsheet program that merely filters applicants on employer criteria: that vendor is not an agent because "the spreadsheet is not participating in the determination of which employees to hire," while "Workday does qualify as an agent because its tools are alleged to perform a traditional hiring function of rejecting candidates at the screening stage and recommending who to advance to subsequent stages, through the use of artificial intelligence and machine learning." She rejected a separate argument, backed by the EEOC, that an AI vendor could be liable as an "employment agency" under Title VII, holding the complaint did not plausibly allege Workday procures candidates for employers, a key component of that definition. The article also notes the practical obstacle to these cases: "Most workers don't know they've been assessed by a discriminatory algorithmic tool or AI."

9042.gloss: Gouchev Law: negotiate indemnity and check liability caps against real risk exposure, and write the internal AI policy before signing the vendor contract
9042.verbatim: Gouchev Law's "10 Critical Clauses for AI Vendor Contracts" argues the real protection in an AI deal sits in an AI Addendum rather than the master services agreement, because "your MSA won't cover what matters most." On liability, the firm notes limitation-of-liability provisions in many AI vendor contracts disclaim indirect, incidental and consequential damages, cap liability at tool fees, and deny indemnity for IP infringement; its guidance is to negotiate robust indemnification coverage for IP infringement claims and data security breaches, look closely at liability caps and damage exclusions, make sure they align with your actual risk exposure, and treat a vendor's refusal of reasonable liability allocation as a factor in vendor selection. It gives a worked example in which an AI-generated deliverable contained an unsubstantiated regulatory compliance claim and, when the client faced penalties, the vendor's liability limitations left the service company carrying all damages and costs. On data, it advises making sure you do not inadvertently grant the vendor rights to use your input for training without written consent, and checking that input is encrypted, isolated, and deleted on termination, aligned with emerging state AI laws including the Colorado Artificial Intelligence Act. It also raises contract misalignment as a distinct risk: map existing client obligations against the AI vendor's license terms before signing, verify you can retain the IP ownership rights clients expect, and confirm you can disclose AI tool usage where client contracts require transparency about subcontractors or third-party tools. Its governance point is sequencing: the internal AI use policy (permitted uses, review processes, data protections, employee training, record-keeping, transparency, usage logs, disciplinary measures) must be written before signing the vendor contract, because internal guidelines shape how you measure compliance with the contract, and the policy should reference the vendor contract's data use, prompt rights and liability clauses so practice does not conflict with the contract.

9043.gloss: Model swap rights: the clause that catches a vendor changing the model under a tool you already audited
9043.verbatim: A widely circulated LinkedIn post by Prem N. lists five clauses every AI vendor contract should include in 2026, framed around the risk that "the vendor may change the underlying model" and "your compliance claims may lack real evidence." The five: (1) data residency, defining where data is stored, processed, backed up and who can access it; (2) model swap rights, meaning visibility and approval rights before the vendor changes the AI model behind the product; (3) output IP, clarifying ownership of AI-generated reports, code, workflows, prompts and business-critical outputs; (4) exit and portability, so you can leave without losing data, workflows, history or operational continuity; and (5) audit access, obtaining evidence through reports, logs, compliance proof and incident records. The post drew 118 reactions and 128 comments. In the comments, a consultant makes the point most relevant to bias auditing: companies assume the system they evaluated initially will behave the same six months later, but once providers silently change models, performance, reasoning patterns and "even compliance characteristics can shift without teams realizing it immediately." Another commenter, Robert Schneider, proposes an additional requirement he expects to become contractual in regulated and high-liability environments: deterministic reconstruction of AI-assisted decisions, meaning the ability to reconstruct the actual decision context at the time of the decision, including model versions, prompts, retrieved context, workflow state, policies and related assets, rather than only receiving logs or compliance reports after an incident. A commenter from IFFAI - Global adds a leverage read on which clauses vendors actually concede in 2026: data residency is increasingly standard and procurement teams win it consistently; audit access is contentious but achievable; output IP is where vendor MSAs are deliberately ambiguous; model swap rights are almost universally not granted, with vendors retaining silent change rights and most procurement teams not even asking; and exit and portability is the most-requested clause that vendors most successfully resist.

9044.gloss: The 14-item AI evidence packet a procurement team can require a vendor to produce on demand
9044.verbatim: In a post on the same LinkedIn thread, Xpert Systems (xpertsystems.ai, 4,640 followers) argues the decisive procurement question for buying AI in 2026 is: "Can your vendor produce, on demand, the documentation our auditor will require?" It rejects "we have a model card and a SOC 2 report" as a sufficient answer and lists 14 items in an auditor-ready packet for a high-risk AI deployment: a model card in the Google/Mitchell style with all 12 sections filled; a system card with capability and limitation evidence; data provenance documentation with the licensing chain; bias and fairness evidence with statistical methodology; robustness testing including adversarial and red-team results; human oversight procedures with intervention logs; incident response and post-market monitoring evidence; PII handling with retention and deletion proof; security controls aligned to your framework (SOC 2, ISO 27001, FedRAMP); explainability evidence per EU AI Act Article 13, Section 1557 or state law; a risk register with severity scoring and mitigation evidence; vendor supply chain documentation including foundation model attestations; lifecycle evidence covering version control and rollback; and training records for personnel touching the system. Its recommendation to procurement teams is to add "AI evidence packet" as a standard procurement requirement, the way SOC 2 is treated today, and it frames a vendor's inability to produce all 14 on request as a procurement risk.

9045.gloss: Refonte Learning (Aug 2026): the corrected Mobley procedural timeline that vendor-governance assumptions now have to account for
9045.verbatim: Refonte Learning's article "Inside the Mobley v. Workday Rulings: What 2026's AI Hiring Bias Case Means for HR Teams," dated Friday, August 14, 2026, sets out the procedural record HR and procurement teams should be briefing executives on, and corrects several dates circulating in summaries. The case is Mobley v. Workday, Inc., Case No. 3:23-cv-00770-RFL, before US District Judge Rita F. Lin in the Northern District of California. In connection with the ADEA collective proceedings, Workday represented that 1.1 billion applications were rejected using its software tools during the relevant period, and Proskauer reported Workday argued the potential group could extend into the hundreds of millions; the article is explicit that this figure describes applications processed or rejected, not 1.1 billion proven instances of discrimination or unique applicants. The corrected sequence: July 2024, the court allowed federal claims to proceed on the theory that Workday was plausibly acting as an agent of employer-clients when performing delegated hiring functions; May 16, 2025, the court conditionally certified a nationwide ADEA collective (not March 6, 2026, as some summaries state); February 17, 2026, plaintiffs' counsel announced court-authorized notice to potential ADEA collective members with an opt-in deadline of March 7; March 6, 2026, the court again rejected Workday's argument that job applicants cannot bring ADEA disparate-impact claims, and dismissed then-pleaded FEHA claims for insufficient California nexus with leave to amend; June 16, 2026 was a hearing, not a ruling, at which Reuters reported Judge Lin appeared skeptical of Workday's position on California law; June 22, 2026, the court largely denied Workday's next dismissal motion after plaintiffs added allegations tying conduct to California; July 1, 2026, an order directed the filing of a Fourth Amended Complaint. The March 6, 2026 order describes the surviving federal disparate-impact claims as race under Title VII, disability under the ADA, and age under the ADEA. Workday has not been found liable on the merits, and no final judgment on whether it discriminated has occurred as of August 14, 2026. The article stresses the distinction for anyone briefing a compliance decision: "the claim survives" is not the same statement as "the defendant discriminated," and the useful question is which assumptions in your vendor-governance model no longer look safe.
